newsitem.title: USA: N. Calif. transit district oks rail project funds.
newsitem.headline: N. Calif. transit district oks rail project funds.

text.p: Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) District Thursday approved a funding agreement with San Francisco International Airport for a portion of a $1.2 billion rail extension project.
Under the agreement, BART Board President Dan Richard said the airport would provide up to $200 million for on-airport improvements related to the massive transit project.
The agreement has already been approved by the San Francisco Airports Commission. The airport funding plan was approved by the Federal Aviation Administration on Oct 18.

The rail extension project stretches BART 8.2 miles southward to four new stations in South San Francisco, San Bruno, the airport and an intermodal station in Millbrae. The total budget for the project is estimated at $1.167 billion.
The BART-airport agreement earmarks $113 million of the $200 million for design and construction of the airport station and aerial trackway.
The remaining $87 million will be used for design and construction of BART systems equipment, including train control, traction power and communications.
"We will be working in very close cooperation with the airport on all aspects of the project as we advance toward opening in the year 2000," BART General Manager Thomas Margro said in a statement.
Richard hailed the agreement with the airport as the means of finalizing local funding for the project.

"This agreement completes the local action that is required before the Federal Transit Administration can notify Congress that its issues have been addressed, which in turn, will trigger a full funding grant agreement being issued by the Federal Transit Administration," Richard said.
The full funding grant agreement, when issued, will be for $750 million, roughly 70 percent of the total project budget.

The San Francisco airport will provide $200 million, the state some $108 million and the San Mateo County Transit District about $99 million. The remaining $10 million would come from bridge funds, project planners said.
